alt: Three parts of the 1559 Settlement: the Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor, the Act of Uniformity required church attendance with a twelve-pence fine for recusants, and some traditional features were kept. Below, tolerance in the 1560s gives way to questions of loyalty after Mary arrives in 1568.
caption: The Settlement asked for outward conformity; Mary's arrival made religion a question of loyalty.

after: ## Mary Queen of Scots: background and challenge
alt: Four options for Elizabeth: freeing Mary, sending her to France or executing her each carried a risk, so Elizabeth kept her in custody for nineteen years. A note explains Mary's claim through Margaret, Henry VIII's elder sister.
caption: Every option was risky, so Elizabeth chose nineteen years of custody.

alt: Two causes, the earls' lost influence and the plan to marry Mary to Norfolk, lead to the rising of November 1569 with Mass at Durham Cathedral, its collapse, and the punishment of the rebels. Its significance: Mary could be a focus for Catholic discontent.
caption: The rising showed that Mary could be a focus for Catholic discontent.

alt: Table of years from 1568 to 1585 pairing Catholic challenges (Douai college, excommunication, seminary priests, Jesuits) with government responses (treason act of 1571, the £20 fine of 1581, the 1585 order expelling priests).
caption: Each new Catholic challenge brought harsher laws.

alt: Vertical timeline: Ridolfi Plot 1571, Throckmorton Plot 1583, Bond of Association 1584, the 1585 Act, Babington Plot 1586, trial at Fotheringhay in October 1586 and Mary's execution on 8 February 1587.
caption: The Bond and the 1585 Act meant Babington's letters could bring Mary to trial.

alt: Three consequences: the main Catholic claimant was removed and the Protestant James VI became heir; Philip II gained another reason for the Armada of 1588; and the Catholic threat at home was reduced.
caption: The execution ended the threat at home but helped bring war with Spain.

alt: The 1559 Settlement sits in the centre, with Catholic pressures (Mary, excommunication, missionaries, plots) pushing from one side and Puritan pressures (vestments, prophesyings, separatists) from the other. A note links religion to the succession.
caption: Religion and the succession were inseparable, and the Settlement was challenged from both sides.
